body_markdown:
On paper, it looked like a great idea. I had to visit Hagerty headquarters in Traverse City, Michigan, from my home in the U.K. for a set of meetings, but flying straight there from London was too simple. It was autumn, and the Great Lakes would be surrounded by the stunning colors of fall, so I hatched a different plan: fly to Toronto, borrow the 1966 Beaumont convertible owned by the Hagerty Canada office, and drive to Traverse City via a ferry to the picturesque Manitoulin Island across Lake Huron. I’d split the journey at motels along the way. What could go wrong?


John Mayhead


John Mayhead


Quite a lot, as it turns out. A five-hour delay at Heathrow meant that I missed my ferry slot, and the following day was fully booked, so before I’d even left the U.K., my route had to change. The delay meant that[Hagerty Garage & Social in Toronto](https://www.garageandsocial.com/location/toronto/) , where the car was stored, would be shut, so the team there very kindly dropped it at valet parking at the airport. But that came with its own challenges: I had nobody to talk me through an unfamiliar car (the headlamp switch took me a while to work out, for instance, and I had no idea how to open the hood). All of which contributed to my[hitting the roads](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/from-malvern-to-the-midnight-sun-in-the-morgan-supersport-400/) in one of the busiest cities in Canada, not only at rush hour on a Friday night, but on the Friday night of Canadian Thanksgiving weekend.


John Mayhead


Now, it’s not the first time I’ve driven in North America. Many years ago, I spent six months in Alberta and British Columbia and bought a beat-up old Chevrolet to drive. Then, in 2008, I worked in the U.S. and even secured my Florida driver’s license, having convinced an official I could drive by circling a car park at the Tampa DMV office as he watched. But the signs, norms, and driving styles take readjustment, and it took me a while to remember that you can turn right on a red light if there’s nothing coming.


The city roads were teeming with traffic, and at first, the light was low and blindingly bright. Then, as dusk fell, I reached Highway 400, packed to capacity, and felt the vulnerability of my tiny rear lights and my thin lap belt as huge slab-fronted trucks thundered past and impatient commuters hustled for position. It took me just under two hours to reach my first night’s destination, a nondescript roadside motel on the outskirts of Barrie, Ontario, on the shores of Lake Simcoe. I was exhausted and glad I was there safely. It hadn’t been much fun, and I was wondering whether this had been a good idea.


John Mayhead


John Mayhead


The car, though, was great.[The Beaumont](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/beaumont/) was a Canada-only model based on the Chevelle and built in Oshawa, Ontario, just a few miles from where I’d picked it up. The model was created by GM as a result of tariff disagreements between Canada and the U..S—ring any bells?—and while the body, chassis, suspension, and powertrain were all Chevrolet Chevelle, the Beaumont gained a unique split front grille complete with twin-maple leaf badge, new rear lights, and a dashboard based on the Pontiac GTO. “Bill,” as I christened the car—you have to be a Brit of a certain age or an England rugby fan to know who Bill Beaumont was—was also the range-topping Sport Deluxe model and twinned a small-block 283-cubic-inch V-8 under the hood, matched up to a two-speed Powerglide automatic transmission. The speedometer was typical of classics of this era: vague, to say the least, but the car pulled really well at all speeds, and the brakes were up to the task.


John Mayhead


John Mayhead


John Mayhead


Day two dawned early, thanks to jet lag. I wrote until around 6 a.m., then went to check on the car. I’d checked the weather forecast before departing the U.K., and it was similar to what I’d left in Sussex: mainly dry and around 20 degrees centigrade—68 for those who use Fahrenheit—but the early morning was cold, and I was surprised not to see the dew that had formed on the windscreen turning to ice. The Beaumont had been freshly serviced and seemed to be in great shape, with the exception of a small oil leak that had been picked up too late to rectify, but other than a few drips, there was no major problem. I went back to the hotel, ate a quick breakfast, checked out, packed my bags into the trunk and set off to fill up with fuel. I’d already noticed that the car was thirsty, but the fuel prices—although at record levels here—were cheap compared with the other side of the Atlantic: I paid $2.14 Canadian per liter for the Supreme 93 RON gasoline, about £1.13 equivalent. I’m used to paying close to £2 per liter back home, although typically for 97 or 99 RON. All of which translates to roughly $5.67 a gallon in the U.S.


John Mayhead


As I pulled onto Highway 400, it was a different place from the previous evening. The traffic was almost gone, and the scenery quickly changed from urban to a rolling expanse of trees, glowing with all the colors from deep red to fiery scarlet. The sun was low and gave the rich light beloved by photographers, soft and warming where it had been harsh the previous evening. I turned on some music: Lord Huron seemed appropriate both in tone and in location. It all made me smile.


John Mayhead


In an hour, I reached my first destination: the small port town of Parry Sound, a natural harbor between the archipelago of islands that dot the eastern edge of Lake Huron. Without trying, I found the dock, where a sightseeing boat was about to leave. I bought a great coffee from a tiny independent kiosk, watched as a float plane made its way out into the bay, then had the first of many conversations that day about the car with a passerby. I unclipped the soft top and watched as the electric motor neatly folded it behind the rear seats. Then I set my map to “avoid highways,” pressed play on the music, and headed out of town.


John Mayhead


It was glorious. The winding roads were empty and flanked with the miles of the trees I’d come to see, interspersed with rocky outcrops and small communities, many of them proudly announcing themselves as First Nation on the ubiquitous roadside billboards. Even when the side roads disappeared and I was forced back on the highway, it was a different place from before: smaller, slower, more beautiful. I pushed on toward Sudbury, and as the kilometers clicked up, I marveled at the size of this lake to my left. “Great” isn’t overstated in this instance: Huron is 183 miles across at its widest—more than the distance between Greece and Libya, across the Mediterranean.


John Mayhead


I was loving the car, too, and fascinated by the comparison with my own grand tourer of the same vintage, a 1967 Lancia Flaminia. The Italian was built for comfort and style, full of leather and chrome and with a sweeping *Superleggera* aluminum body created by Touring of Milan. It was made for navigating the twisting roads of the Apennines and cruising next to the shores of Lake Garda. The Beaumont was all about power: Although the 283 (4.7L) engine was the smallest fitted to the Sport Deluxe model, it dwarfed the Lancia’s 2.8 liters, and the immediacy of power puts it a league above in a straight line. Inside, though, you understand that lightness and production cost were prioritized over luxury: The dash is plastic, the panels stamped and tinny. All the money has gone into making this thing powerful, in looks as well as performance. The handling is ideal for the big roads I was driving here: You kind of drift into turns, correct, then drift a little back again. The auto gearbox is perfect, too, because you just push it into drive and forget about it until you next stop.


John Mayhead


John Mayhead


That night, I reached a motel in the small town of Blind River. I’d joined the Trans-Canadian Highway (“Trans-Can”) just after Sudbury; it skirted the north shore of Huron, but until the town, the trees had prevented a good view out across the lake. I parked the Beaumont, checked in, then took a walk down to the shoreline. The view was impressive, and the sun gave the last of its light through a cloudy sky, glinting off the water. In the far distance was Manitoulin Island, where I’d originally planned to drive, and to its right, an expanse of water that met the horizon with no sign of Michigan beyond. Walking back and finding the restaurants shut, I bought some food at a supermarket and retreated to my motel room.


John Mayhead


Before dawn, I checked the fluids and tires, packed my kit, set the satnav and the playlist, and rumbled off down the highway. I use that word—rumble—by design: the V-8 provides a constant deep and reassuring growl, and as the roads were totally empty and the conditions good, I was able to push the car a little as the sun rose behind me.


John Mayhead


The colors were glorious again. The rich early light played in the trees and across the rare fields and deep red Gambrel barns that had started to appear as the forests gave way to farmland. To my left, I glimpsed the deep blue of inlets that showed through the trees, and I was finally tempted to stop at a small harbor and watch the sun rise across the water.


John Mayhead


An hour later, I entered the border town of Sault Ste. Marie—the Rapids of Saint Mary—a place the First Nation Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) people called Bawating, or “The Place of the Rapids.” It was well named as the point joining Lake Superior with Lake Huron, some six meters lower, but today the St. Marys River rapids have mostly been tamed to provide hydroelectric power, with a series of locks, too, for shipping. The town also seemed tame, and for the first time since Toronto, I was truly out of the wilderness and into a regular layout of blocks, traffic lights, and fast food outlets.


John Mayhead


Sault straddles the border, and I followed the signs south, crossing between twin Canadian and U.S. flags halfway across the bridge spanning the river, and my map app announced I’d made it to Michigan. A mile or so further, and I arrived at the U.S. immigration station, where, as a Brit driving a Canadian-registered car into America, I was told to pull over. U.S. immigration officials have a stern reputation worldwide, but today it was unwarranted: They were fascinated by the car and very friendly. The officer asked me where I’d come from, then, a little suspiciously, asked why I’d driven up via Sault rather than the direct route to Traverse City south of Huron. Before I could answer, he looked at the car and said, “Oh yes, the car. I get it…” and stamped my passport.


John Mayhead


Tolls paid and the top now down as the day started to heat up, I drove south on I-75, soon passing over the Mackinac Bridge, with Huron on my left and Lake Michigan stretching away to my right. As I reached land, I turned off right onto Highway 31, choosing the longer (but what I hoped would be) more picturesque route along the coast via Petoskey. I wasn’t disappointed. The autumnal colors were still as vibrant here as they had been in Ontario but were now mixed with the fruit farms that Northern Michigan is famous for. The roads, too, had changed, with traffic more plentiful and noticeably populated by more premium vehicles. Every other car seemed to be a range-topping truck, a vast RV trailer, or a Corvette. I started to see European cars for the first time, too: a Porsche 996 Turbo surprised me, as did an immaculate MGA with a raked, racing windscreen that was parked outside a convenience store.


John Mayhead


In Petoskey, I stopped for a break at a lakeside viewpoint and was immediately approached by a couple of guys who wanted to ask about the car. I was used to this by now. In Canada, too, it seemed that every time I stopped, someone wanted to talk about the Beaumont or take a photograph, but here in Michigan the interest was extraordinary, and at one point, I had two men in line to talk to me. I have this a little with my Lancia back home, and I love talking about cars, so I was happy to chat; I truly think that this trigger for human interaction is what makes this hobby so great.


John Mayhead


I drove the final few miles down into Traverse City and, with mixed feelings, pulled into the hotel. I’d driven just over[600 glorious miles](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/according-to-you-our-longest-road-trips/) in this wonderful car, and it hadn’t missed a beat. I was tired, but I’d discovered towns and villages, views and roads that I’d remember forever. For a few days at least, it was over and I’d miss it. But in short order, I’d be on the road again, this time heading south toward Detroit, before turning west back to Toronto and my flight back to the U.K.


*Huge thanks to Nicholas Keith of Hagerty Canada and the rest of his team, who made this road trip possible by preparing and delivering the car, and by supporting me with answers to my persistent questions whilst on the road.*
